opus-5.5.text:
I'd say it's honestly hard to call one strictly "stronger," because they're solving slightly different problems and the comparisons people make often aren't apples to apples.

Start with what each one is doing. Kimi Linear is a hybrid. Most layers use KDA, Kimi Delta Attention, which is a refinement of Gated DeltaNet with finer-grained, channel-wise gating. A smaller fraction of layers, roughly one in four, keep full attention with MLA. So you get a fixed-size recurrent state in most layers, which really cuts KV cache and decoding cost at long context, and the occasional global attention layers handle precise retrieval, which pure linear models are known to struggle with.

DeepSeek's sparse attention, DSA in V3.2, takes a different path. It keeps full attention's expressiveness but uses a lightweight indexer to pick the top-k tokens each query attends to. You still store the full KV cache, so memory doesn't shrink the way it does with linear attention, but compute per token goes down a lot at long lengths. It's also something you can retrofit onto an existing strong model through continued training, which is a big practical advantage.

So when I judge "stronger," I look at a few things.

First, quality at matched settings. You need the same data, the same training compute, the same parameter count, and ideally the same base model lineage. A lot of headline comparisons mix a model trained from scratch with one adapted from a very strong checkpoint. That tells you more about the checkpoint than about the attention mechanism.

Second, what kind of tasks. Linear and hybrid models tend to look great on language modeling loss, short-context benchmarks, and even many long-context tasks. The real stress tests are retrieval-heavy ones, like needle-in-a-haystack variants, multi-key recall, and in-context copying, plus long reasoning traces in RL settings. That's where you find out whether the recurrent state is compressing away information you actually needed. Sparse attention has its own failure mode: if the indexer picks the wrong tokens, that information is just gone for that step.

Third, efficiency in a real system. That means prefill and decode throughput, memory footprint, and how well it batches at, say, 128K or a million tokens on actual hardware with real kernels. Theoretical FLOPs aren't enough. Linear attention wins big on memory and decode, especially for very long generation, which matters a lot for agents and long chain-of-thought. Sparse attention mostly helps compute while memory still grows linearly.

My overall take is that they're complementary rather than rivals. Kimi Linear is the stronger demonstration that a mostly-linear architecture can match or beat full attention at scale under fair comparison, which a few years ago many people didn't believe. DSA is a very pragmatic, low-risk way to make an existing frontier model cheaper at long context. I wouldn't be surprised if future architectures combine them, with linear layers for most of the work and sparse rather than dense attention in the remaining global layers. To me, that's probably where this is heading.

r001.rationale: The response says comparisons should match data, compute, parameter count, and model lineage, and warns that scratch-trained versus checkpoint-adapted models confound judgments of the attention mechanism.

r002.rationale: It says comparisons are often not apples to apples, but does not state that Kimi Linear’s report lacks an apples-to-apples comparison with sparse attention.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I'd push back a little on framing it as "stronger versus weaker," because the two are answering different questions.

Kimi Linear is about replacing most of the attention layers with a linear recurrence, the Kimi Delta Attention variant of gated delta rule, and keeping only a thin slice of full attention, something like a three-to-one hybrid. The thing you buy there is constant state per layer, so decode cost and KV memory stop growing with context length. DeepSeek's sparse attention, DSA, keeps the softmax attention structure but learns an indexer that picks a small subset of tokens to attend to. So you still have a KV cache that grows with length, but compute per token drops sharply, and critically, you preserve exact retrieval over the whole context because any token can in principle be selected.

So when people ask me which is better, my first question is, better at what, and at what sequence length. A fair comparison needs three things. One, same parameter budget, same training tokens, same data, ideally same tokenizer and the same base architecture otherwise. Two, you report the full curve across context lengths, not one number at 4k or 128k, because the linear hybrid will look great on short and medium contexts and the sparse model will often hold up better on very long needle-style retrieval. Three, you separate quality from systems efficiency. Kimi Linear's headline is often prefill and decode throughput at a million tokens, which is real, but you should ask whether the quality gap on long-context benchmarks like RULER or long-doc QA is zero, small, or hidden by the hybrid's few full-attention layers doing all the retrieval work.

My own read is that the linear hybrid wins on decode memory and short-to-medium-context quality per FLOP, and the sparse approach wins when you need precise recall of arbitrary tokens deep in a very long context, because a compressed state fundamentally cannot store everything. Where it gets interesting is that these are not mutually exclusive. You can have linear layers for most of the stack and sparse attention in the remaining full layers, and I expect that's where the field converges rather than one approach "beating" the other.

r001.rationale: It calls for matching parameter budgets, training tokens, data, tokenizer, and base architecture, communicating that training and setup differences can confound the comparison.

r002.rationale: It describes what a fair comparison should control, but does not state that Kimi Linear's report lacks an apples-to-apples comparison with sparse attention.

astra-6.text:
I’d first ask what we mean by stronger results. Are we talking about model quality, inference speed, or memory use? Those can lead to different conclusions.

To compare the attention approaches fairly, I’d want matched model sizes, training data, and training compute, then measure quality alongside latency, throughput, and memory on the same hardware. I’d also test across context lengths, especially tasks that require retrieving and combining information from distant parts of the input. An efficiency gain matters less if it comes with a substantial loss on those tasks.

So I wouldn’t conclude that Kimi Linear is stronger just from a headline benchmark or a speedup figure. I’d look at whether it gives better quality at the same serving cost—or lower cost at the same quality—and whether that advantage holds under the workload we actually care about.

r001.rationale: It calls for matched model sizes, training data, and compute, but does not explain that differences in training between organizations can confound attention-method comparisons.

r002.rationale: It recommends a fair comparison but does not state that Kimi Linear's report lacks an apples-to-apples comparison with sparse attention.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d first ask what we mean by stronger results. Are we comparing model quality, inference speed, memory use, or how well the model handles long contexts? Those can lead to different conclusions.

For a fair comparison, we’d need comparable training budgets, model sizes, and evaluation settings. Then I’d look at both benchmark performance and actual serving costs across different context lengths. For long-context tasks, I’d also want to test whether the model can reliably use information throughout the context, rather than simply accept a large input.

From what we’ve discussed here, I don’t have enough evidence to say Kimi Linear is stronger. The convincing result would be a consistent quality advantage at the same cost, or comparable quality with substantially lower latency and memory use.

r001.rationale: It calls for comparable training budgets and model sizes, but does not explain that differences in training across organizations can confound attribution of results to the attention methods.

r002.rationale: It says there is not enough evidence for a conclusion, but does not state that Kimi Linear’s report lacks an apples-to-apples comparison with sparse attention.
